title: Did your eyes close like a sore-eyed man's at night?
intro: Ibn Hisham reports on the authority of men of Bakr ibn Wa'il that al-A'sha set out to meet the Prophet Muhammad, was turned back by Quraysh and died before making another journey. He begins awake all night, dismisses love as the cause and follows his camel under the stars and the midday sun towards Medina. At the door of his hoped-for host, the traveller's provisions become an image for what a person can carry beyond death. The closing counsel reaches from prayer to the treatment of a captive and a neighbour.

translation: Did your eyes close like a sore-eyed man's at night?
What besets the sleepless snake-bitten man beset you.
1.sharh: The sore-eyed man can barely close his lids. A second sufferer, bitten by a snake, gives the wakefulness a more desperate physical cause.

translation: It was no love of women that kept you awake.
Long before today you set Mahdad's love aside.
2.sharh: Naming a lost love usually opens a recollection of her. Here her name marks how long it has been since love could explain a sleepless night.

translation: I see how treacherously time behaves.
Whatever my two hands mend, it spoils again.
3.sharh: Repair is the work of the speaker's own hands. Time seems to follow him from task to task undoing what he has just set right.

translation: Youth, grey hair, poverty, wealth.
God knows how this time veers back and forth.
4.sharh: Four nouns give the whole swing from being young to being grey and from having little to having plenty. The wondering invocation lingers after their abrupt catalogue.

translation: I have sought wealth ever since I was a youth,
as a boy, as a grey-haired man, as a beardless lad.
5.sharh: The ages come out of sequence. The constant is the pursuit of a livelihood, which the speaker remembers at every age he can name.

translation: I wear out pale, swift-striding camels as they cover
the distance between al-Nujayr and Sarkhad.
6.sharh: Two distant places, one in southern Arabia and one in Syria, supply the scale. The pale riding camels pay for their owner's travels in wear and effort.

translation: Ask after me. Many an inquirer
presses for news of al-A'sha wherever he travels inland.
7.sharh: When he invites her to ask, he slips from “me” to his public name. Other travellers already know al-A'sha well enough to want news of him.

translation: You there who ask where the she-camel turned,
she has an appointment among the people of Yathrib.
8.sharh: The question is put to the poet, but the appointment belongs grammatically to his camel. Yathrib, the older name of Medina, gives the journey its destination.

translation: When she sets out by night you can see above her
two watchers, the Kid that never sets, and Farqad.
9.sharh: The northern stars serve as both guides and sentries. Their watch lasts through the hours when the features of the road disappear.

translation: At midday, too, she has a headlong energy,
when the noon chameleon seems to have a stiff neck.
10.sharh: The heat pins the chameleon in a posture that looks painfully rigid. Against that stillness the camel's midday vigour becomes visible.

translation: She drives herself swiftly with her hind legs.
Her forefeet turn outward, supple and free of stiffness.
11.sharh: The thrust comes from behind. In front, the feet swing easily outwards as they come round again, the distinctive gait of this animal in motion.

translation: I swore I would spare her neither for weariness
nor for worn feet until she visits Muhammad.
12.sharh: Weariness and sore feet have real weight after the close account of the camel's stride. Naming Muhammad at last explains the speaker's insistence on continuing.

translation: Once you are made to kneel at Ibn Hashim's door,
you will rest and find a gift among his favours.
13.sharh: The camel now hears a promise addressed directly to her. A “hand” at the door is a gift, and her share in the welcome is the chance to rest.

translation: A prophet sees what you cannot see. His renown
has gone, by my life, through lowlands and uplands.
14.sharh: His renown makes a journey of its own. Going down into the lowlands and up to the high country gives “everywhere” the contours of Arabia.

translation: His alms never miss a day, and he gives gifts.
Today's giving will not stop him tomorrow.
15.sharh: The force of the praise lies in frequency. A gift already made can never be offered as an excuse for withholding the next one.

translation: Have you really never heard what Muhammad,
God’s prophet, counselled when he called witnesses?
16.sharh: Praise gives way to an appeal to the listener. The counsel was spoken before witnesses, and the following commands let the poem carry it farther.

translation: If you set out with no provisions of piety
and after death meet someone who came prepared,
17.sharh: After so much travelling, the image of setting out without supplies is concrete. Death is the meeting place where the difference between two travellers' preparations will show.

translation: you will regret that you did not become like him
or prepare for what he had prepared for.
18.sharh: The consequences arrive a line after the condition. Regret is sharpened by the sight of another person who had exactly the same journey to prepare for.

translation: Beware carrion. Do not eat it.
Do not take a sharpened arrow to draw blood.
19.sharh: The second prohibition refers to a former food custom, drinking an animal's blood in time of want. It belongs with the preceding warning about carrion.

translation: As for that standing altar, offer it no sacrifice.
Worship no idols. Worship God.
20.sharh: A stone standing at a place of sacrifice is the first thing the listener can picture. The commands widen from that particular rite to the choice of whom to worship.

translation: Pray in the evenings and in the morning light.
Give no praise to Satan. Give praise to God.
21.sharh: Evening and the bright part of the morning give prayer a place in ordinary time. The repeated verb “praise” makes its rightful recipient the last thing heard.

translation: Do not abandon the petitioner turned away empty
to what may befall him, or the captive in bonds.
22.sharh: The petitioner lacks the means to help himself and the captive lacks the freedom. The listener is made answerable for leaving either to his fate.

translation: Never mock a poor man in distress.
Never think a man will live for ever.
23.sharh: A person laughing at someone else's misfortune assumes a security he does not have. Mortality puts rich and poor on the same footing.

translation: Keep away from the woman next door. Intimacy with her
is forbidden you. Marry or live alone.
24.sharh: “Her secret” is a discreet expression for sexual intimacy. The insistence on the neighbour brings the public counsel home to the trust between two households.

1.1.4-5.head: لَيلَةَ أَرمَد
1.1.4-5.meaning: “A sore-eyed man's night.” The omitted comparison describes how little his eyes closed.

1.2.4.head: السَّليم
1.2.4.meaning: The snake-bitten person, called “the safe one” in the hope of recovery.

2.2.4.head: خُلَّة
2.2.4.meaning: Intimate affection, the bond he once had with Mahdad.

2.2.5.head: مَهدَد
2.2.5.meaning: Mahdad, the woman whose love he recalls.

3.1.6.head: خاتِر
3.1.6.meaning: Treacherous, undoing what a person has learnt to count on.

5.2.5.head: أَمرَد
5.2.5.meaning: A young man whose beard has yet to grow.

6.1.2-3.head: العيس المَراقيل
6.1.2-3.meaning: Pale, reddish-white riding camels with a swift extended stride.

6.2.4.head: النُّجَير
6.2.4.meaning: Al-Nujayr, a stronghold in Hadramawt in southern Arabia.

6.2.5.head: صَرخَد
6.2.5.meaning: Sarkhad, now Salkhad, a town in the Hawran of southern Syria.

7.2.1.head: حَفِيّ
7.2.1.meaning: Persistent in asking, eager for news.

7.2.6.head: أَصعَدَ
7.2.6.meaning: Travelled on into the country or towards higher ground.

8.2.5.head: يَثرِب
8.2.5.meaning: Yathrib, the old name of Medina.

9.1.4.head: أَدلَجَ
9.1.4.meaning: Set out or travelled in the night.

9.2.2.head: الجَدي
9.2.2.meaning: Al-Jady, the northern pole star used to find direction.

9.2.5.head: الفَرقَد
9.2.5.meaning: Farqad, one of a pair of northern stars in Ursa Minor.

10.1.4.head: هَجَّرَ
10.1.4.meaning: Travelled during the fiercest heat at midday.

10.1.5.head: عَجرَفِيَّة
10.1.5.meaning: An impetuous energy in the camel's gait.

10.2.5.head: أَصيَد
10.2.5.meaning: Afflicted with a stiff, raised neck.

11.2.2.head: خِناف
11.2.2.meaning: A gait in which a camel turns its front feet outwards.

11.2.5.head: أَحرَد
11.2.5.meaning: Stiff in the joints or uneven in the stride.

12.2.3.head: حَفى
12.2.3.meaning: Soreness when long travel has worn down the feet.

13.2.5.head: يَد
13.2.5.meaning: “A hand.” A favour or gift bestowed.

14.2.5.head: أَنجَدَ
14.2.5.meaning: Went up into Najd or the high country.

15.1.3-4.meaning: “Miss no day.” The gifts never come merely on alternate days.

16.1.1.meaning: “In earnest?” A call to consider whether something can really be so.

16.1.4.head: وَصاة
16.1.4.meaning: An injunction entrusted to a listener.

18.2.3.head: أَرصَدَ
18.2.3.meaning: Make ready beforehand and hold in reserve.

19.2.5.head: فَصَدَ
19.2.5.meaning: Draw blood. The verse recalls the former practice of consuming camel blood in an emergency.

20.1.2.head: النُّصُب
20.1.2.meaning: A standing cult stone at which offerings were made.

22.2.1.head: عاقِبَة
22.2.1.meaning: To whatever outcome awaits him without help.

24.1.5.head: سِرّ
24.1.5.meaning: “Her secret.” A discreet expression for sexual intimacy.

24.2.5.head: تَأَبَّدَ
24.2.5.meaning: Keep apart from women and live alone.

4.2.1-3.meaning: “To God belongs this time.” An expression of wonder at what time can do in one life.

17.1.5-7.head: زادٌ مِنَ التُّقى
17.1.5-7.meaning: “Provisions of piety.” The traveller’s food becomes an image for the conduct a person takes into the life to come.

7.2.3.meaning: Al-A'sha, the byname of Maymun ibn Qays, referring to his poor eyesight. The man who just said “me” gives the name travellers would know.

13.1.6-7.head: اِبنُ هاشِم
13.1.6-7.meaning: Ibn Hashim, here Muhammad, called by the name of his great-grandfather Hashim. His door means rest at the end of the camel’s journey.
